This is the "Master Backend Prompt" designed to build the entire FastAPI ecosystem for your civic grievance platform. It integrates the geographic data from your KML, the official councillor records from your PDF, and the categorization logic from your workflow diagrams.

Project Specification: CivicConnect Smart Backend (FastAPI)

Role: You are a Senior Backend Engineer and Geospatial Data Expert. Objective: Develop a production-ready FastAPI application to power a multi-tenant civic grievance system partnered with MCD Delhi.

1. Core Tech Stack & Setup

  • Framework: FastAPI with uv for package management.

  • Database: PostgreSQL with PostGIS extension for geospatial queries.

  • ORM: SQLAlchemy (Async) or Prisma.

  • Geospatial Engines: geopandas, shapely, and fiona for processing the official Delhi Ward KML.

2. Database Architecture (Ref: Unified Schema)

Implement the following tables based on the established DBML:

  • Administrative: zones, wards (linked to KML boundaries), departments.

  • Users & Auth: citizens, officers (with hierarchy levels), and a polymorphic sessions table for JWT-based auth.

  • Grievances: grievances (lat/lng, category, status), grievance_media, and audit_logs.

  • Governance Mapping: Integrate the 250 Ward Councillors and their party affiliations directly into the wards table.

3. Specialized API Logic & Endpoints

A. The "Smart Report" Engine

  • Endpoint: POST /complaints/create

  • Logic: 1. Accept lat, lng, category, and image_stream. 2. Point-in-Polygon Lookup: Use the delhi_wards.kml data to automatically identify the ward_id and zone_id. 3. Councillor Association: Automatically attach the relevant Ward Councillor details (Name/Party) to the report for the user's dashboard. 4. Auto-Assignment: Route the ticket to the specific officer assigned to that Ward and Category.

B. The "10-Meter" Worker Protocol

  • Endpoint: PATCH /tasks/{id}/status

  • Logic:

    1. Verify the worker’s current GPS coordinates.

    2. Calculate the distance to the original complaint's coordinates.

    3. Strict Enforcement: Reject the update if the distance is > 10 meters. Return a 403 Forbidden with a "Not at Site" message.

C. Analytics & AQI Dashboard

  • Endpoint: GET /analytics/ward-hotspots

  • Logic: Aggregate complaints by ward boundaries to generate a heatmap.

  • Hyper-Local AQI: Create a stub for the ML-based pollution source detection, allowing for "Automated Tickets" if AQI thresholds are breached in a specific ward.

4. System Requirements

  • File Handling: Securely store "Live-Captured" images in S3 or local storage, strictly validating that they are not uploaded from a gallery.

  • Middleware: Implement a custom CORS middleware to support the Multi-Column Web Dashboard and the Responsive Mobile App.

  • Categories: Seed the database with the Sanitation, Infrastructure, Public Health, and Horticulture categories from the master mindmap.

Implementation Roadmap

  1. Environment Setup: Initialize with uv and configure the PostGIS connection.

  2. KML Migration: Write the one-time script to parse delhi_wards.kml and populate the wards table with geometry.

  3. PDF Data Import: Bulk-import the 250 Councillor Records into the database.

  4. Endpoint Development: Prioritize the "Smart Report" and "10-Meter" logic.

You said

write a python program that converts gpkg to geojson

Gemini said

To convert your optimized GeoPackage (.gpkg) data into a web-friendly GeoJSON format, you can use the following Python program. This is particularly useful for the frontend of your CivicConnect app, as most web mapping libraries like Leaflet or Mapbox consume GeoJSON directly.

Python Program: GPKG to GeoJSON Converter

Python
import geopandas as gpd

def convert_gpkg_to_geojson(input_gpkg, output_geojson):
    try:
        print(f"Reading {input_gpkg}...")
        # 1. Load the GeoPackage
        # Since GPKG can contain multiple layers, geopandas reads the first by default
        gdf = gpd.read_file(input_gpkg)

        print(f"Converting to GeoJSON...")
        # 2. Export to GeoJSON
        # We use 'utf-8' to ensure names like 'Fateh Nagar' are encoded correctly
        gdf.to_file(output_geojson, driver='GeoJSON', encoding='utf-8')
        
        print(f"Success! Saved {len(gdf)} features to {output_geojson}")

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error during conversion: {e}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Assuming you followed the previous step to create delhi_wards.gpkg
    INPUT_FILE = "delhi_wards.gpkg"
    OUTPUT_FILE = "delhi_wards.geojson"
    
    convert_gpkg_to_geojson(INPUT_FILE, OUTPUT_FILE)

How to Run it

Since you are using uv on your MacBook Air, execute the script with:

Bash
uv run main.py

Why this is useful for your 2026 Project

  • Frontend Integration: While you use GPKG for high-speed backend lookups in your FastAPI app, GeoJSON is the standard for rendering the Ward Boundaries on the user's mobile and web dashboards.

  • Coordinate Precision: This script preserves the high-precision longitude and latitude coordinates found in your original delhi_wards.kml file.

  • Data Portability: GeoJSON is a plain-text format, making it easy to inspect your Ward Names and Population Data without needing specialized GIS software.

Gemini said

To extract data from this specific GeoJSON structure, you can use the built-in json library in Python. This script iterates through the features list, pulls the administrative data from the properties object, and the spatial data from the geometry object.

Python Program: GeoJSON Data Extractor

Python
import json

def extract_ward_data(geojson_str):
    # Parse the GeoJSON string into a Python dictionary
    data = json.loads(geojson_str)
    
    extracted_records = []

    # Iterate through each feature in the collection
    for feature in data.get('features', []):
        properties = feature.get('properties', {})
        geometry = feature.get('geometry', {})

        # Extract specific fields
        ward_no = properties.get('Ward_No')
        ward_name = properties.get('WardName')
        coordinates = geometry.get('coordinates')

        # Store in a list of dictionaries
        extracted_records.append({
            "Ward_No": ward_no,
            "Ward_Name": ward_name,
            "Coordinates": coordinates
        })

    return extracted_records

# --- Example Usage ---
# Use the GeoJSON string you provided (clipped for brevity here)
geojson_input = """
{
"type": "FeatureCollection",
"features": [
{ "type": "Feature", "properties": { "Ward_No": 100, "WardName": "FATEH NAGAR" }, "geometry": { "type": "MultiPolygon", "coordinates": [[[[77.1033165, 28.6343911], [77.10335, 28.63419]]]] } }
]
}
"""

results = extract_ward_data(geojson_input)

for ward in results:
    print(f"Ward #{ward['Ward_No']}: {ward['Ward_Name']}")
    print(f"Sample Coordinate: {ward['Coordinates'][0][0][0]}")
    print("-" * 30)

Why this is useful for your 2026 Project

  1. Frontend Integration: This script allows your FastAPI backend to process raw GeoJSON uploads and convert them into structured records for your PostgreSQL/PostGIS database.

  2. Ward Identification: Once you extract these coordinates, you can use the shapely library (as we discussed previously) to perform the Point-in-Polygon checks that power your automated ward-tagging feature.

  3. Data Cleanliness: Notice how the script uses .get(). This is defensive coding; it prevents your backend from crashing if the MCD (Municipal Corporation of Delhi) provides a file where some optional fields (like TotalPop) are missing.

Pro-Tip for GeoJSON

Since your GeoJSON uses MultiPolygon, the coordinates are nested deeply: [ [ [ [lng, lat], ... ] ] ].

  • Layer 1: MultiPolygon list.

  • Layer 2: The specific Polygon.

  • Layer 3: The Linear Ring (the boundary).

  • Layer 4: The individual Point.

get the string from json file

Gemini said

To extract the Ward Number, Ward Name, and the Coordinates string directly from a file on your disk (like delhi_wards.json), use this implementation. It uses Python's json library to parse the file and json.dumps if you specifically need the coordinates formatted back as a string for your database.

Python Script: JSON File Extractor

Python
import json

def extract_from_json_file(file_path):
    try:
        # Open and load the JSON file from disk
        with open(file_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
            data = json.load(f)
        
        extracted_data = []

        # Iterate through the GeoJSON features
        for feature in data.get('features', []):
            props = feature.get('properties', {})
            geom = feature.get('geometry', {})

            ward_no = props.get('Ward_No')
            ward_name = props.get('WardName')
            
            # Get coordinates as a raw object
            coords = geom.get('coordinates')
            
            # If you need the coordinates specifically as a JSON string for your DB:
            coords_string = json.dumps(coords)

            extracted_data.append({
                "Ward_No": ward_no,
                "Ward_Name": ward_name,
                "Coords_String": coords_string
            })
            
        return extracted_data

    except FileNotFoundError:
        return "Error: The file was not found."
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return "Error: Failed to decode JSON. Check the file format."

# --- Execution ---
FILE_PATH = "delhi_wards.json"  # Ensure your file is named this or change it here
results = extract_from_json_file(FILE_PATH)

if isinstance(results, list):
    for entry in results:
        print(f"PROCESSED: Ward {entry['Ward_No']} ({entry['Ward_Name']})")
        # Printing first 50 chars of the coordinate string as a preview
        print(f"COORD STRING PREVIEW: {entry['Coords_String'][:50]}...")
        print("-" * 40)
else:
    print(results)

Technical Breakdown for your MCD Delhi App:

  1. File Loading: We use with open(...) which is the safest way to handle files on your MacBook Air to ensure the memory is cleared after reading.

  2. json.dumps() vs json.loads(): json.load reads the file into a Python dictionary. json.dumps (used inside the loop) converts the coordinate list back into a string, which is exactly what you need if you are saving this to a standard text or JSONB column in PostgreSQL.

  3. Handling MultiPolygons: Since your data uses MultiPolygon, the string will contain the full nested array structure [[[[long, lat], ...]]]].

Gemini said

To convert your extracted ward data into a CSV file, you can use Python’s built-in csv module. Since your data is already structured as a list of dictionaries, csv.DictWriter is the most efficient choice for a Senior AI Engineer to implement.

Python Script: Ward Data to CSV Converter

Python
import csv
import json

def save_wards_to_csv(data, output_filename):
    if not data:
        print("No data to save.")
        return

    # Define the headers based on your dictionary keys
    fieldnames = ['Ward_No', 'Ward_Name', 'Coords_String']

    try:
        with open(output_filename, 'w', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as csvfile:
            writer = csv.DictWriter(csvfile, fieldnames=fieldnames)

            # Write the header row
            writer.writeheader()
            
            # Write all ward rows
            writer.writerows(data)
            
        print(f"Success! Data saved to {output_filename}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"An error occurred while saving CSV: {e}")

# --- Integration with your existing loop ---
# results = extract_from_json_file("delhi_wards.json")

# Convert and Save
save_wards_to_csv(results, "mcd_wards_data.csv")

Important Technical Note on Coordinates

In your snippet, you used ward['Coords_String'][0][0][0]. Since we used json.dumps() in the previous step, Coords_String is a String, not a list.

  • For the CSV: The code above will save the entire coordinate block as a single text cell.

  • For Analysis: If you want to access a specific point (like the first longitude), you must use the raw list object before stringifying it, or use json.loads(ward['Coords_String']).

Why this is optimal for your MCD Project:

  1. Excel Compatibility: By using utf-8 encoding, ward names like "Fateh Nagar" or those containing special characters will open correctly in Excel or Google Sheets.

  2. Database Seeding: This CSV is now in the perfect format for a bulk COPY command into your PostgreSQL wards table that we designed in the DBML section.

  3. Data Portability: You can easily share this CSV with the MCD Delhi officials for verification without requiring them to run Python scripts.

Here is the master prompt for your AI agent (Antigravity/Codeium/Cursor):

Role: Senior Full-Stack Lead (Flutter & FastAPI Specialist)

Objective: Complete the end-to-end integration between the Flutter Frontend and the FastAPI Backend using the provided openapi.json. You must implement a production-grade communication layer that prioritizes User Experience (UX) and Data Integrity.

1. Core Architectural Tasks

  • Service Layer Generation: Using the openapi.json, generate or update all API service classes. Use dio or http with interceptors to handle global authentication headers.

  • State Management Integration: Connect every meaningful widget to the backend. If a widget displays data (e.g., Ward Councillor name, total complaints in Ward 100), it must fetch this from the API.

  • Theme Synchronization: STRICT REQUIREMENT: Every new UI element (loaders, error states) must match the Citizen Portal's design system (colors, border radii, typography).

2. UX & Feedback Engineering

  • Skeleton/Shimmer Loading: Replace all static "Loading..." text with shimmer effect placeholders that match the shape of the upcoming data (e.g., list tile skeletons for the grievance feed).

  • Granular Loading States: Implement individual loading indicators for specific actions (e.g., a small circular progress indicator inside the "Clock-In" button while the attendance request is pending).

  • Global Error Handling: * If the backend returns a 400 or 500 error, show a user-friendly SnackBar or Toast.

    • Logic Specifics: If the worker attempts to resolve a task and the backend returns a "Not at Site" error (due to the 10-meter proximity rule), show a specific high-visibility warning with the distance remaining.

  • Input Validation: Map backend validation errors (e.g., 422 Unprocessable Entity) directly to the relevant form fields in Flutter.

3. Production Features

  • Pull-to-Refresh: Add RefreshIndicator to all major list views (Grievance Feed, Task List).

  • Optimistic UI: Where safe (like upvoting a complaint), implement optimistic updates to make the app feel instantaneous.

  • Connection Resilience: Implement basic retry logic for failed requests and show a "No Internet Connection" banner if the device is offline.

4. Technical Constraints

  • File Handling: Ensure the "Live-Capture" image flow correctly multi-parts the image to the FastAPI POST /complaints/create endpoint.

  • Zero Functional Loss: Do not remove any existing frontend logic. Enhance it.

  • Performance: Ensure no widget rebuilds unnecessarily during API calls.

Implementation Strategy for You:

  1. Feed the openapi.json: Upload the file to the agent's context first.

  2. Run in Batches: I recommend asking the agent to "Integrate the Auth and Attendance flow first" and then "Integrate the Grievance Reporting and Ward Lookup flow." This prevents context window overflow.

  3. Skeleton Loading: If you don't have a shimmer package, tell the agent: "Use the shimmer package from pub.dev for placeholders."

Here is the master prompt for your AI agent (Antigravity/Cursor/Codeium):

Role: Senior Full-Stack Architect (Geospatial & Dashboard Specialist)

Objective: Build a comprehensive Admin Command Center (Web optimized) for the MCD Civic Connect platform. This panel serves as the "God-view" for municipal administrators to monitor the city's health, filter by jurisdiction, and track officer efficiency.

1. Core Layout & Design System

  • Theme: Strictly adhere to the Citizen Portal's white and teal-green palette. Use a multi-column "Responsive Dashboard" layout.

  • Navigation: Persistent Left Sidebar containing: Global Overview, Map View, Ward Analytics, Officer Management, and System Logs.

  • Responsiveness: Optimize primarily for Desktop Web (1080p to 4K) using a sidebar-content-panel split.

2. Geospatial Intelligence Module (The Map)

  • Integration: Implement a high-performance map (Google Maps or Mapbox).

  • Boundary Layers: Load the delhi_wards.geojson. Render all 250 ward polygons with a thin teal stroke.

  • Live Markers: * Plot grievances as coordinate-specific points.

    • Color Code Markers: Red (Unassigned), Amber (In Progress), Green (Resolved).

    • Cluster Mapping: Use marker clustering for high-density areas.

  • Heatmap Toggle: Provide a toggle to switch from markers to an AQI/Complaint Density Heatmap based on ward boundaries.

3. Hierarchical Filtering System (The Command Engine)

Implement a "Smart Filter Bar" that updates the map and data tables in real-time:

  • Zone Filter: Select by MCD Zone (North, South, East, West, etc.).

  • Ward Filter: A searchable dropdown of all 250 Wards. Selecting a ward should "Fly-To" that specific polygon on the map.

  • Councillor Overlay: When a ward is selected/clicked, show a persistent "Ward Info" card featuring the Councillor Name, Political Party, and Population Data extracted from the database.

  • Status/Date Filters: Filter by "Open vs Closed" and "Date Range."

4. Data Grid & Management

  • Unified Grievance Table: A sortable, searchable data grid. Each row must show: ID, Ward, Category, Assigned Officer, and a "View Proof" button (to see the live-captured photo).

  • Officer Tracking: A separate view showing all field workers. Indicate their "Attendance Status" and their current distance from assigned tasks.

  • Export Module: Ability to export filtered ward data (e.g., "All Open Waste issues in Fateh Nagar") into CSV/PDF.

5. Technical Logic & API Integration

  • Backend Communication: Use the openapi.json to generate the service layer.

  • State Management: Use Riverpod or BLoC. Ensure that changing a filter in the sidebar instantly updates the Map markers AND the Data Table without a full page reload.

  • Geofencing Feedback: Visually flag any task updates where the worker was outside the 10-meter requirement (Audit Log).

I need a prompt that every other portal should resemble like in citizen portal in flutter

Gemini said

To ensure your AI agent replicates the "Citizen Portal" DNA across the Worker and Admin portals with 100% fidelity, you need a prompt that establishes the Citizen Portal as the Design System Master.

Here is the professional, architect-level prompt for your AI agent:

Role: Lead UI/UX Flutter Architect

Objective: Implement absolute visual and structural parity across all application portals (Worker Dashboard, Admin Command Center) based on the existing Citizen Portal. You are responsible for ensuring a unified "CivicConnect" brand identity.

1. The Design Master (Single Source of Truth)

  • Reference: The Citizen Portal is the master reference for all UI/UX.

  • Directive: You must replicate the exact Typography (font sizes, weights), Color Palette (Primary Teal Green: #008080, Background White: #FFFFFF), Border Radii, and Elevation/Shadow patterns used there.

  • Component Sync: If a specific "Grievance Card" or "Status Badge" exists in the Citizen Portal, use the exact same widget structure and styling for the other portals.

2. Adaptive Layout Architecture

  • Responsive DNA: Replicate the 100% responsive behavior of the Citizen Portal.

  • Navigation Parity: * Web: Mirror the Left-side Sidebar navigation pattern. Convert any bottom bars from mobile views into these sidebars.

    • Mobile: Maintain the Bottom Navigation Bar with identical icon styling and active-state highlights.

  • Multi-Column Logic: All portals must use the same grid-based multi-column layout on desktop view to ensure a consistent administrative feel.

3. Interaction & Feedback Standards

  • Loading States: Use the same shimmer or CircularProgressIndicator styles used in the Citizen Portal.

  • Form Design: Inputs, dropdowns (Ward/Zone filters), and buttons must use the identical InputDecoration and ButtonStyle themes.

  • Map Styling: Any map implementation must use the same Teal-themed custom map style and polygon stroke widths established in the master view.

4. Technical Constraint

  • Centralized Theming: Do not hardcode colors or sizes. Rely on the existing ThemeData or a global AppTheme class to ensure that a change in the master theme ripples through the Citizen, Worker, and Admin portals simultaneously.

Why this prompt works for your project:

  1. Eliminates "Design Drift": By using terms like "DNA replication" and "Master Reference," you prevent the AI from trying to "improve" or change the look of the Admin or Worker sections.

  2. Forces Scalability: It requires the AI to look at your ThemeData. Since you have 250 wards to manage, having one theme control all three portals is the only way to maintain the app long-term.

  3. Branding Consistency: It ensures the MCD Delhi teal-and-white identity is professional and uniform, whether the user is a citizen reporting a pothole or an admin viewing a heatmap.
